title: Itinerary Reconstruction
statement:
Order a set of one-way flight tickets into a single trip that uses every ticket exactly once and is alphabetically smallest.

Contract
- Each ticket is a two-element list `[from, to]` of airport codes. The trip begins at `start`.
- Every ticket must be used exactly once; the same ticket may appear several times and then must be used that many times.
- A valid trip is guaranteed to exist. With no tickets the trip is just `[start]`.
- Return the airports visited in order. When several valid trips exist, return the one that is smallest when compared airport by airport using normal string order.
- Do not modify the ticket list.

Examples
- `[SEA-PDX, PDX-SEA, SEA-LAX]` from `SEA` returns `[SEA, PDX, SEA, LAX]`; flying to `LAX` first would strand the remaining tickets.
- `[AAA-BBB]` from `AAA` returns `[AAA, BBB]`.
- `[HUB-CCC, HUB-AAA, AAA-HUB, CCC-HUB]` from `HUB` returns `[HUB, AAA, HUB, CCC, HUB]`.

examples.input: tickets = [HUB-CCC, HUB-AAA, AAA-HUB, CCC-HUB], start = HUB

hints: Using every ticket exactly once is an Eulerian path: edges are tickets, airports are nodes. Greedily taking the smallest destination can strand tickets behind a dead end.

Keep each airport's destinations in sorted order. Walk forward taking the smallest unused ticket; an airport with no tickets left can only be the last stop of what remains, so it is finalised and placed at the back.

Hierholzer's algorithm: DFS with a stack, pop an airport into the answer when it has no unused tickets, then reverse the answer. Use an explicit stack to avoid deep recursion. Intended complexity: O(E log E) time to sort or heapify destinations and O(E) space for E tickets.
inputSyntax: Input: start airport, then tickets as FROM>TO (uppercase codes), for example: SEA SEA>PDX PDX>SEA SEA>LAX
